passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Hemant, Class 10, asked to see me in his free period. He was angry and said so: the library shuts at 3:30 for students who take the colony bus, while day scholars from town may stay until 5.
He had not shouted at the librarian. Instead he had kept a page for three weeks with dates, times and who was sent out. Omkar, a day scholar, had signed under it to say he had seen it happen.
I told Hemant his anger was fair, and that a written page would carry further than a raised voice. We drafted a short request asking the principal to review the rule, and he chose to hand it in himself.
The rule was made for bus timings, and I doubt anyone had noticed its effect. I will ask for a reply by next week.
Mr. Rane

qa.q: For how many weeks had Hemant kept his page of dates and times?
qa.a: He had kept it for three weeks.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was angry: he said so, and he spent three weeks recording each incident instead of letting it pass.

qa.q: What could Hemant do if the principal does not reply?
qa.a: He could ask Mr. Rane and his allies such as Omkar for help in taking the facts to the next formal complaint route.

qa.q: Why might the principal have made the rule without noticing its effect?
qa.a: The rule was made for bus timings, so the principal may not have seen that it sent the colony students out of the library while day scholars could stay.

grounding: A school rule treats students who take the colony bus unfairly; Hemant documents facts, gets an ally's signature and uses the formal request route.
